content.thinking:
I'll write the whole file carefully in one pass without testing, designing a whimsical capybara: chubby barrel body about 1 meter long, blocky head with a rounded snout, tiny ears and eyes, short dumpy legs with webbed toes, plus a small round songbird perched on its head for extra charm.

Now I'm planning out the coordinate system and proportions, with the body facing forward and sized for exaggerated chubbiness, then building a skeleton with hip, spine, neck, and head joints positioned along the body's curve.

I'm sketching the tail as a short two-joint chain parented to the hips, then working through how the body loft should run along the spine chain, figuring out where the path stations need to start relative to the hips joint position.

Writing loft station values...

Adding more measurements for leg length and head placement, estimating overall body proportions for a stubby, whimsical capybara shape. Now I'm working out the fur color palette, defining a warm brown base with countershading between back and belly for a cel-shaded look.

Checking the Paint instance case confirms the shadow falls back to resolving lit against position and normal. Now I'm shaping the capybara's blocky head using a loft along z with stations from skull to blunt muzzle, widening then narrowing toward the nose, and adding a nose pad sphere near the tip to capture that characteristic large, flat capybara snout.

Adding darker nose with tiny nostril spheres, a separate lower jaw sweep attached to its own bone, cream-brown coloring for the jaw, and small white box teeth peeking out at the front for a whimsical touch.

Now working on eye placement: positioning big glossy dark eyes high on the sides of the head with white highlight spheres and brow ridges, checking how the head loft's surface width narrows at that z-position to get the placement right.

Next I'm adding small round ears at the top back of the head, scaled spheres in brown with pinkish inner spheres, tilted to orient naturally against the skull.

Settling on a direction roughly [s*0.7,0.3,0.1] for the ears, keeping it symmetric since orientation sign doesn't really matter here. Now I'm thinking about adding fur tuft cards scattered over the body for texture—around 250 small tapered-strand shapes, leaning at about 70 degrees, using a tinted paint color to give the brown fur its texture while still reading as a simple SVG tuft shape.

For the fur texture itself I'm keeping the base strand white-ish with a darker centerline so the paint tint multiplies in nicely, filtering cards on the body by normal direction so they don't scatter onto the underside, and adjusting lean/size for cards on the body versus sparser, smaller ones on the head. I'm also planning thin whisker capsules near the muzzle, three per side, running from a base point near the head bone out to a tip, colored dark or cream with a small radius.

Now I'm working out the front leg rig: picking hip, knee, and foot positions on the body, checking the distances against the intended segment lengths so the limb chain closes properly, and naming the joints shoulder, elbow, and wrist for the IK chain.

For the side naming, I'm mapping the sign of my s variable to left/right labels based on which way +X points in this space. Then I'm wiring up parenting for each leg chain—front legs attach to the chest joint in the spine, hind legs attach to the hips—and setting bend-direction hints so elbows bend backward and hind knees bend forward like a capybara's, before placing the hind hip and foot target points.

The hind limb has three segments summing to about 0.31, with the target distance around 0.255, well within reach so the IK solves without issue; with four points I get four joint names (hip, knee, hock, foot) following the one-more-name-than-spans convention, and I'm noting the last segment runs roughly parallel to the root-to-target line.

Still writing leg sweep code...

For the feet, I'm thinking about capybara anatomy—webbed toes, four on front feet and three on hind feet—and planning to represent each toe as a small dark capsule angled forward from the ankle, giving that semi-aquatic look.

I'll resolve the foot joint by picking the last joint in the chain (or the tip if present), and give the lower legs a darker mottled brown gradient color while keeping the flat color count within limits.

For the face, I'm adding soft pink cheek discs and a rounded dark nose sphere near the muzzle tip, but noticing the head's loft ends further out than intended due to the round cap's radius extending the dome past z=.78 toward .9 — I need to pull the last station back to around z=.72 to keep proportions correct.

Checking the head and body caps more carefully, both ends seem to be ballooning past where I want them — the head's rounded cap pushes the nose/back further than planned, and the body's forward cap domes out enough to overlap where the head sits. Since capybaras lack a distinct neck, I think this overlap can actually work as a natural chest-to-head transition rather than something to fully eliminate.

I'll shorten the body's last station and adjust its cap dimensions so the dome ends sooner, letting the head start slightly inside the body for a continuous forehead-to-shoulder line instead of a separate neck. Now I'm plotting the neck joint positions and spine path coordinates to connect everything smoothly.

Mapping out the neck and head joint hierarchy next — neck1 and neck2 parented to the spine, head parented to neck2 with aim direction toward the front, and a jaw joint hanging off the head with its own aim point. I'm noting that joints need both position and aim values, and that a jaw with no child bone is fine since other examples handle it the same way — skipping a separate jaw-tip joint for simplicity.

Now I'm working out the head's paint treatment: a mottled cel-shaded base color with a lighter cream tone fading in along the muzzle and underside near the chin, using a fur-edge gradient based on position and axis to blend the colors smoothly.

For whimsy, I'm adding a small chubby songbird perched on the capybara's head — giving it its own joint hierarchy separate from the main rig, with body, head, tail, wing, and beak joints each as simple one-joint chains, colored in bright yellow and teal to pop against the fur.

Adding tiny leg rods sinking body toward the head, plus small flattened orange toe spheres, then placing the head sphere forward with a red cap paint.

I'm shading the head with a countershaded gradient for cap versus cheek color, adding tiny black eye spheres with white highlights, and shaping a small cone beak.

Modeling the tail feathers...

Defining joint coordinates...

Adding wing stripe patterning, then moving to small head crest spikes and cheek blush details to round out the bird's facial features.

I'll add a mottled orange-yellow paint for the yuzu with a tiny green leaf, then give the capybara a small grass stalk sticking from its mouth, attached near the jaw with a tiny seed head. For body markings, I'll keep the reddish-brown with lighter belly and consider a subtle dark dorsal stripe.

For the tail, since capybaras barely have one, I'm just adding a tiny nub sphere on a one-span chain attached near the base of the spine. Then I'll name the roles clearly: spine, neck, and tail, so each chain is easy to reference later.

Now I'm figuring out toe placement for front and hind feet, using small capsule shapes offset from each limb's end position to create a webbed, slightly overlapping toe look, with the front getting four toes at tighter spacing and the hind getting three.

I'm adding dark nail tips at each toe end plus a flattened, elongated sphere for the foot pad itself, positioning it so its bottom sits flush with the ground, and assigning dark skin tones to the feet distinct from the furred lower legs.

Checking ground clearance: toe tips sit just a hair above the floor, which is negligible, and the leg cap ends slightly below zero which is also within tolerance. Then I'm placing the nose as a scaled dark sphere near the head's dome tip, with tiny black nostril spheres positioned symmetrically on either side.

I'm realizing the overall body length looks too long once I add up the rear cap, body, and nose extension—roughly 1.4-1.5m, more than a real capybara. I could shift the rear station inward and shrink its radius to pull the dome back, keeping the head's forward reach the same, to bring proportions closer to realistic scale.

Now I'm working out the body station positions along the spine, placing hip joints for the hind and front legs relative to those station widths so the legs root at sensible points on the torso.

For the face, I'm adding sleepy half-lid eyes using a hemisphere cap over each eye sphere, tilted slightly outward, to give that whimsical droopy-eyed capybara expression.

Working out the eye highlight position—placing a small white sphere offset toward the front and slightly below center so it peeks out from under the lid, and positioning the lid hemisphere just above the eye center to cover the upper half while leaving the highlight visible in the lower portion.

I'm checking that the head's cross-section width at that height is enough for the eye to protrude slightly outward—confirms it sticks out about .026 beyond the surface, which looks right. Now placing the cheek blush as a flattened pink sphere, positioning it along the surface curve near the cheek area.

For the ears, I'm computing their position at the top-rear of the head using the surface height formula, then adding an inner ear detail offset forward from the outer ear sphere. I'm also noting I'll skip detailed brow lines since the sleepy lid already conveys enough expression, and starting to think about scattering fur/card tufts across the body surface with a minimum distance constraint.

Estimating body surface area to pick a scatter count around 300 cards with a .04 minimum spacing between them, I'm setting up the paint logic to read position and normal at each card root and filter out cards pointing too far downward. For the head, I'm scattering fewer cards (around 80) with filters to keep normals pointing upward and positions away from the nose and eyes, sizing them slightly smaller than the body cards. I'm deciding to skip whisker and chin hair details, then moving on to the leg fur tufts.

Now I'm setting up imports -- builder, limb IK, RNG, catmull path, paint utilities (countershade, mottle, paint), SVG texture, and toon shading (cel, furEdge) -- making sure each one maps to actual uses like wing bars and bird countershading, then starting the metadata block with name, description, and a "whimsical" style tag.

Building the capybara's build function with a root hips joint and starting the spine chain using catmull-spline points...

Adding jaw joint parented to head, then setting up the tail chain and body loft using the spine bone with coat color stations. I'm looping over left/right sides to build front legs with limb() calls, passing root/target points and bend directions, checking that array inputs work fine as PointInput for the API.

Now I'm working out the chain setup for each front leg — naming joints shoulder/elbow/wrist, assigning them a "leg" role, parenting to the spine, and setting contact points before moving into the sweep geometry generation...

Defining hind leg points...

Now I'm thinking through the foot, taking the last joint of the leg chain as the foot bone, then writing a helper function that adds a flattened heel sphere plus a set of toe capsules spread evenly across the foot width.

Adding more skeleton joints...

Now I'm setting up the bird's paint colors with countershading, and checking the geometry placement—eyes and beak positioned relative to the head sphere center to make sure they sit correctly on the surface without clipping through.

Adding more bird parts...

Still working out leaf geometry...

I'm checking jaw placement next — adding a capsule shape with a cream-brown tone, making sure its radius doesn't push it outside the head's lower boundary near the snout.

Then I'm positioning two small white box shapes as teeth, sized and placed so they sit just below the upper lip line and above the jaw's front edge.

I'm adding a nose sphere scaled to a flattened shape, nostrils as tiny spheres, and whisker sets of three per side made from thin flat-capped rods colored a warm brown, plus small whimsical touches like blush marks and a tail tuft. For texturing the cards, I'm starting on an SVG definition.

Working through the leg and card helper functions, checking types for hits and scatter params, and setting up colors for legs using a mottled dark brown cel shading, considering whether to gradient darker toward the foot.

Now I'm figuring out a whimsical mouth decoration — thin dark curve lines near the nose that sweep along the head's surface to suggest a smile, working out approximate coordinates where the curve should sit on the dome of the head at different z-depths.

Rather than compute exact surface positions, I decide to use a drape function to snap the smile path onto the head surface with a slight lift, then sweep it as a stroke using the ink color. Mentally I run through the final checklist of what's used—joint, rng, catmull, limb, countershading, mottle, paint, svg, cel, furEdge, ink—confirming nothing is unused before writing the file.

For the wing I'm alternating paint colors based on x-position bands to create a striped pattern, and using countershading wrapped in cel shading for the body. For the tail I'm setting up a two-point chain attached at the hips with proper joint naming, then preparing to write out the full file with consistent leg naming conventions across sides.

For the legs I'm using a sweep with positional radius arrays to taper the shape. For the body I'm deriving a surface card from the already-built body geometry, making sure the body is fully constructed before extracting its surface. Ready to write the complete definition now.
